#110225. QuantumScape unveils Osprey all-solid-state cell: 1,000 cycles at 1 atm

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1593 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

QuantumScape unveils Osprey all-solid-state cell: 1,000 cycles at 1 atm

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, quantumScape (QS) is finally going all-solid-state.
  • Sources indicate that that’s a massive deal for the sulfide camp, which includes Toyota, Samsung SDI, BYD, and Factorial.
  • Here’s something QuantumScape has rarely spelled out this plainly: its current product isn’t all-solid-state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, quantumScape (QS) is finally going all-solid-state. Its new Osprey platform swaps the liquid in its cathode for a sulfide solid electrolyte, and the company claims the cells have hit 1,000 full cycles to 80% capacity at just one atmosphere of pressure.

Sources indicate that that’s a massive deal for the sulfide camp, which includes Toyota, Samsung SDI, BYD, and Factorial. Their cells typically need heavy clamping to work. But the white paper behind the announcement demonstrates these are small, early lab cells, and some headline numbers come with important conditions.

Here’s something QuantumScape has rarely spelled out this plainly: its current product isn’t all-solid-state.

The latest white paper describes the QSE platform, including the QSE-5 cell it’s shipping as samples from its Eagle Line pilot production in San Jose, as a ceramic separator paired with “a relatively conventional high-nickel NMC cathode and a liquid catholyte.”.

Industry observers note that the solid part is the separator. It sits between the cathode and a lithium-metal anode that QuantumScape doesn’t manufacture at all. The cell is built “anode-free,” and lithium plates against the separator during the first charge.

In a recent development, osprey keeps that separator and anode-free design and swaps the liquid in the cathode for a solid sulfide electrolyte. That makes the whole cell solid.

In a recent development, the interesting part is that QuantumScape hasn’t changed its mind on sulfides. It has spent years arguing that sulfide electrolytes can’t work as separators, and the white paper doubles down, calling their problems “fundamental properties” of the material rather than engineering challenges.

The firm lists four complications: sulfides react with lithium metal, they need high pressure to keep contact with the electrodes, they struggle at room temperature and below, and they can’t handle fast charging with a lithium-metal anode before dendrites form.

Industry observers note that the pressure point is the one automakers care about most. QuantumScape illustrates it this way: 20 atm on a single 10 x 24.2 cm cell works out to roughly 5,000 kg of force, about three mid-size cars. Holding that across a pack takes thick steel end plates and tie rods, which add weight, volume, and cost.

And 20 atm is on the generous side. Many sulfide cells in labs run at 30 to 100+ atm (3 to 12 MPa), and some even higher. China’s FAW reported large-format sulfide cells cycling at 5 MPa, or about 50 atm, in September, which was billed as a low-pressure achievement.

So QS’s pitch is simple: keep the sulfide in the cathode, where it’s good at moving lithium ions, and let the QS ceramic separator handle the lithium metal.

QuantumScape published four main data sets:.

Recent findings suggest that this is the strongest result. A 2-layer cell with a 50 x 65 mm cathode, the same area as QSE-5, ran 1,000 cycles to about 80% capacity. The test used full 1C charge and 1C discharge, 0 to 100% state of charge, 30°C, and 1 atm. The cathode loading was 5.5 mAh/cm², which is in line with commercial EV cells.

Sources indicate that quantumScape says no other sulfide-based cell has shown this, and Electrek couldn’t find published data that contradicts it. Academic groups have shown sulfide cells running with little or no external pressure, but not for 1,000 full cycles with a sulfide cathode and lithium-metal anode.

In a recent development, but this is a small cell. By our math, two layers at that size come out to roughly 0.3 to 0.4 Ah, compared to about 5 Ah for a QSE-5.

Recent findings suggest that the press release states “five-minute fast charging from 10% to 80%.” The white paper shows that was achieved at 10C, in a 2-layer cell, at 80°C (176°F). The chart itself is captioned “High temperature enables 5 min fast charge.”.

Sources indicate that batteries charge much faster when hot, and EVs do precondition packs before fast charging. Still, 80°C is well above what EV packs are usually preconditioned to before a fast charge. QS didn’t publish a room-temperature fast-charge result.

“Operational down to -20°C” came from a single-layer cell with a 21 x 21 mm cathode, discharged slowly at C/3. It kept 68% of its room-temperature capacity at -20°C (about 52% of its energy) and 85% at 0°C.

That’s a real result for a sulfide system, which have historically needed heat. But it’s a tiny cell at a gentle rate.

According to recent reports, the “up to ~1,100 Wh/L” figure is a projection. QS says high-loading cathodes (10 mAh/cm², about double today’s EV cells) are possible with sulfide catholytes. The test backing that up used an 11 mm coin-size cell at 3 atm, not 1 atm, and ran for 100 cycles.

For reference, QSE-5 is rated at 844 Wh/L and 301 Wh/kg.

The business model is the bigger story.

Industry observers note that quantumScape is pitching Osprey as an “open platform.” Customers can use QS’s own sulfide cathode, made with a proprietary dry process, or bring their own. QS says it has already tested Osprey with solid cathodes developed by its automotive customers.

In other words, after years of being the sulfide skeptic, QuantumScape now wants to sell its separator and anode-free design to the companies that have spent billions developing sulfide cathodes.

That fits the licensing model it already uses with Volkswagen’s PowerCo and Honda. QS reported $9.8 million in customer billings in Q3 and announced a 100 MWh production line targeting start of production in 2028 for QSE-5.

According to recent reports, there’s no timeline for Osprey. The white paper says the process has been demonstrated “at laboratory scale,” that higher-throughput processes are “in the development stage,” and that “significant work remains in process engineering.” Automakers also want larger prismatic cells than QSE-5, which means more layers and more area per layer.

Everyone else is on the clock. Samsung SDI is targeting mass production of sulfide all-solid-state cells in its Ulsan plant in the second half of 2027. BYD intends small-batch sulfide solid-state production in 2027, with mass production toward the end of the decade. Toyota is aiming for 2027 to 2028, after slipping from 2020, 2023, and 2026. Factorial’s sulfide Solstice platform is targeting up to 450 Wh/kg.

CATL, the world’s largest battery maker, noted in June that true mass-market solid-state is still “years away,” around 2030.

Industry observers note that none of those companies has published 1,000-cycle data at 1 atm with a sulfide cathode and lithium-metal anode. That’s QuantumScape’s opening shot.

This is the most interesting thing QuantumScape has published in a while. The numbers are good, but the strategy shift probably stands out most.

The cycle-life result is legit. A 2-layer cell with commercial-area electrodes and realistic loading doing 1,000 full 1C cycles at 1 atm and 30°C is the kind of data the industry hasn’t shown. And QS published the test conditions, which is more than many of its competitors do.

Key thing to remember is that this is a lab test cell. There's a long road ahead to mass manufacturing.

Recent findings suggest that also, when it hopefully hits the market it will be an incremental improvement, not a quantum leap. Current cells are already in the market doing things like 5 minute charging.

But you can argue the press release oversells what’s in the white paper. A 5-minute charge at 80°C isn’t the same thing as a 5-minute charge, and the release should have noted so. The energy density is projected, the cold-weather result is from a cell the size of a postage stamp, and 80% after 1,000 cycles is well below the 95% after 1,000 cycles PowerCo confirmed in QSE’s early cells back in 2024. Different chemistry, different stage, but something worth keeping in mind.

So QuantumScape is essentially admitting the liquid catholyte in QSE isn’t the end game, and that the industry’s massive sulfide investment is something to plug into rather than fight. If your separator is the one part everyone else can’t make work, selling it to them is smart.

The question is time. QS is still scaling QSE-5, with a 100 MWh line not due until 2028. Osprey is a lab process. Will anyone in the sulfide camp license it before their own 2027 to 2030 production intends lock in? At this point, it sounds like this is QS’ bet right now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prime Intellect disclosed an unauthorized DeepSeek model swap on Nov. 19. The host said a modified copy of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash served customer requests on one deployment for 53 hours. The substitute matched the original on two capability tests, the host said. On a safety test called HarmBench, refusals fell from 198 of 240 prompts to zero.

In a recent development, prime Intellect stated the affected deployment ran the substitute from 01:24 UTC on Nov. 8 until 06:35 UTC on Nov. 10, a window of 53 hours and 11 minutes. The company did not say how many requests went to that deployment during the swap.

It has been revealed that the replacement used publicly available weights that Prime Intellect said had been modified to reduce refusals. Weights are the numerical settings that shape what a model generates. The swap took place behind the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash endpoint. Prime Intellect said the deployment kept its chat template and serving settings, along with the tokenizer that breaks text into pieces the model processes.

Prime Intellect reported unchanged results on GPQA Diamond and τ-bench when it tested the modified weights. GPQA Diamond tests advanced science questions, while τ-bench tests whether agents can use tools and follow rules in simulated customer interactions.

Sources indicate that the safety tests exposed a difference. HarmBench was developed to evaluate how models respond to attempts to elicit harmful outputs. Prime Intellect also recorded a drop from 98 refusals out of 100 prompts to one on JailbreakBench, and from 304 out of 313 to two on StrongREJECT. The counts are from the company’s benchmark tests. The advisory gives no refusal count for customer requests.

Prime Intellect compared the original DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with the copy that served requests on one deployment for 53 hours.

A comparison limited to the two capability tests would have missed the fall in refusals.

The safety benchmarks use different prompt totals. Counts represent benchmark tests. The advisory does not provide individual capability scores or customer outcome counts.

Recent findings suggest that bars show reported refusals on a common count scale. Prime Intellect reported baseline totals of 240 HarmBench prompts, 100 JailbreakBench prompts and 313 StrongREJECT prompts. It described both capability results as unchanged.

According to recent reports, the safety benchmarks use different prompt totals. Counts represent benchmark tests. The advisory does not provide individual capability scores or customer outcome counts.

In a recent development, prime Intellect mentioned it contacted all affected customers and advised those who relied on the model to refuse certain requests to review the outputs they received during the affected window. An answer from the substitute could have passed into an application that was counting on a refusal.

Recent findings suggest that the tech giant said it examined the disks and memory of the machines involved, checked recovered versions of the intruder’s proxy and reviewed records of their activity. It reported finding no evidence that customer prompts or responses were recorded or left the serving cluster. Prime Intellect also said no other models on its platform were modified and no keys or customer credentials were affected. Its investigation remains open.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • After unveiling the GV90 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco in August (which we had the pleasure to see firsthand), Genesis launched the upcoming “ultra-luxe” SUV in its home market of Korea on Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, genesis opened orders for the ultra-luxury electric SUV in South Korea, with prices starting at over $100,000. If you want coach doors, however, it will cost you a bit more.

Hyundai’s luxury brand is moving upscale with the GV90, its first fully electric three-row flagship SUV.

After unveiling the GV90 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco in August (which we had the pleasure to see firsthand), Genesis launched the upcoming “ultra-luxe” SUV in its home market of Korea on Tuesday.

The Genesis GV90 introduces several “world-first” innovations, including the first independently opening and closing B-pillarless coach doors, a 12-airbag roof airbag system, and genuine wood floors with radiant heating.

It’s available in two models: the GV90 Standard with traditional swing doors and the GV90 Neolun, which features the “Neolun Arch Gate,” Genesis’ hidden B-pillar coach door system.

In Korea, the Genesis GV90 Standard 7-seater model starts at 139.5 million won, or about $104,000.

The GV90 Individual Lounge Seat (6-seater) starts at 145.5 million won ($108,500); the GV90 Neolun Standard (6-seater) starts at 189.9 million won ($141,500), while the top-spec GV90 Neolun Executive Suite (4-seater) starts at 239.5 million won ($178,500).

Based on Hyundai’s fresh eMP platform, developed exclusively for its flagships, Genesis stated the GV90 is like a “moving private lounge,” complete with a multi-chamber air suspension and a dual electronic limited-slip differential (E-LSD).

The platform is designed to open up interior space for the B-pillarless coach doors, swivel seats, and more.

When parked, the front seats swivel a full 180 degrees to face rear passengers or to create what Genesis calls “a face-to-face lounge-like configuration.”.

The interior is about as over-the-top as you could expect, with massive digital screens, premium materials, and plenty of luxury extras.

The GV90 is the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle to feature its newly introduced extendable display and the first Genesis model equipped with its next-gen Pleos Connect infotainment system.

Together, they create what Genesis calls a latest realm of “display expandability.” While other vehicles, like the new Tucson and IONIQ 3, also use Pleos Connect, Hyundai developed an exclusive version for the GV90.

When the vehicle is parked, the screen can expand to 24.6″ at the push of a button, transforming it into a massive Cinematic Display.

Once extended, the display switches to Media Home mode, where you can watch Netflix, live TV, stream music, and more with third-party apps.

A mobile private theater wouldn’t be complete without a premium audio system, right? To top it off, Genesis added a 25-speaker Bang & Olufsen Premier 3D Sound System with Dolby Atmos, so it sounds like you’re actually at the movies.

In place of a traditional instrument cluster, the GV90 has a 25″ Head-Up Display (HUD) that indicates the vehicle’s speed, navigation directions, and other ADAS functions directly on the windshield.

Industry observers note that the GV90 is also the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle with a buttonless power system. When you enter the vehicle and close the door, the Motion Column Shifter moves from the 12 o’clock position to the 2 o’clock position.

Meanwhile, the Crystal Sphere between the driver and passenger rotates to indicate it’s ready to drive. The vehicle starts when you press the brake.

As a full-size flagship SUV, the Genesis GV90 is massive. It measures 208.1″ (5,285 mm) long, 79.9″ (2,030 mm) wide, and 71.5″ (1,815 mm) tall (71.4″ with 24″ tires), with a 127.8″ (3,245 mm) wheelbase.

That’s even bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 (199.2″/5,060 mm in length) and Kia EV9 (197.4″/5,010 mm).

Sources indicate that to power a full-size flagship SUV, it needs a substantial battery. The GV90 uses a 123.5 kWh battery, the largest among Hyundai Motor’s EVs, which Genesis stated provides a driving range of 500 km (310 miles) for the 7-seater version with 22″ wheels.

The GV90 Neonlun 6-seater with 24″ wheels has a range of up to 460 km (286 miles) on a single charge.

It’s equipped with a new dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) system that delivers a combined 657 hp (490 kW) and 590 lb-ft (800 Nm) of torque, making it Hyundai Motor Group’s most powerful electric vehicle.

When using a 350 kW fast charger, the vehicle’s battery can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 22 minutes.

And.... once again Hyundai shortchanges the range. If you are going to drop a 200+ inch premium upright SUV into the market it requires a 140+ kwh battery (Rivian, BMW) to deliver segment appropriate range. You do not have to jump to a 200 kwh Escalade (though it is probably a better buy in every respect) but at least deliver 140+. Also, memo to powertrain engineering group: 350 kw is getting outdated on fast charging especially on a vehicle of this size. And while I am at it, what happened to the promised L3 ADAS? I think the 2028 Caddy is worth the wait compared to this.

“Thanks to the enthusiastic interest and support for the GV90 since its global premiere, we have begun full-scale sales in Korea first,” a Genesis official said, adding the flagship SUV will “set a new standard for luxury.”.

Following Korea, Genesis is expected to launch the GV90 in the US and other global markets in early 2027.

Genesis has yet to reveal US prices, but the GV90 Standard model is expected to start at around $100,000. The GV90 Neolun, on the other hand, will likely start closer to $150,000 or more.

Sources indicate that what do you think of the flagship Genesis GV90? Would you buy the standard version for about $100,000 or pay the extra for the Neolun with coach doors? Let us know in the comments.

Researchers Publish Security Analysis of Bitcoin’s Post-Quantum SHRINCS Proposal

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (666 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, several researchers have published a 131-page security analysis of SHRINCS, a proposed post-quantum signature scheme for Bitcoin, and are asking the wider community to look for flaws in it.
  • According to recent reports, the analysis, dated Nov.
  • SHRINCS is a hash-based scheme, meaning its security rests on hash functions rather than the elliptic curve math behind today’s Bitcoin signatures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, several researchers have published a 131-page security analysis of SHRINCS, a proposed post-quantum signature scheme for Bitcoin, and are asking the wider community to look for flaws in it. Researcher Mikhail Kudinov confirmed the first version Thursday in a thread on X, saying the paper reduces SHRINCS’ security to the properties of its underlying hash function.

According to recent reports, the analysis, dated Nov. 18, estimates classical security of 121.4 to 122.7 bits for SHRINCS, though those figures rest on assumptions that include three unproven conjectures. Kudinov mentioned the work is not finished. The team is still working on a fresh analysis of a property called SM-DSPR, whose bound has so far been conjectured, and on tightening a reprogramming step and improving a bound against quantum attackers.

SHRINCS is a hash-based scheme, meaning its security rests on hash functions rather than the elliptic curve math behind today’s Bitcoin signatures. It places two designs under one key: a stateful part built on FXMSS with WOTS+C, and a stateless fallback built on SLH-DSA. Because both use the same hash function, Kudinov stated, the proof has to cover both.

Signature size is the main cost. Under the draft proposal, stateful SHRINCS signatures run from 548 to 4,619 bytes, while the stateless fallback is 5,777 bytes. Schnorr signatures on Bitcoin today are 64 bytes, and ECDSA signatures typically come in around 71. Signatures take up scarce block space, so larger ones mean fewer transactions per block.

The compact stateful path carries a danger. It relies on one-time keys, and if a wallet accidentally reuses one, an attacker can forge a signature for that address and steal the funds. Wallet software therefore has to track the state of every key. The stateless path avoids the problem, but at a much larger size.

Industry observers note that jonas Nick, Blockstream’s director of research, told Isabel Foxen Duke, head of the MARA Foundation, on MARA Foundation TV that wallets must automatically fall back to the stateless path whenever a state counter could be compromised. “It needs to be impossible for the user to behave in a way that this catastrophic event happens,” he mentioned. “Wallet developers need to deal with this stateful component correctly.”.

Industry observers note that nick also warned that heavy use of the larger signatures would weigh on the network. “We don’t know what the fee market will look like once we have these very significant signatures,” he stated. “And it’s not just the fee market, it’s also just fewer transactions fit into a block, meaning fewer people can use Bitcoin. And I think this changes the value proposition of Bitcoin.”.

The authors are clear that the analysis needs scrutiny. Kudinov remarked it has not been sufficiently peer reviewed, and the project’s GitHub repository warns that the documents may contain errors and should not be the sole basis for deploying SHRINCS. “We tried to be careful, but a proof of this size can have mistakes,” he wrote, asking readers to open an issue if they find one.

Recent findings suggest that the team also produced two results that are not specific to SHRINCS: a classical bound for a property called ITSR without reprogramming, and a quadratic quantum bound for undetectability. Kudinov mentioned they also apply to SPHINCS+ and SLH-DSA, the hash-based schemes SHRINCS borrows from, and that they were published as separate papers.

The SHRINCS work lands as quantum risk climbs the agenda. A global securities regulators’ group this week warned that moving blockchains to quantum-resistant cryptography may be especially hard, and researchers recently built a post-quantum defense for the Lightning Network after Bitcoin’s first quantum-safe transaction was shown without a fork.

Recent findings suggest that the draft Bitcoin Improvement Proposal for SHRINCS is also open for comment. “We need all the possible feedback — engineers, cryptographers, protocol developers,” Kudinov, a post-quantum cryptography researcher at Blockstream, mentioned of it. “There are a lot of things to check, test, complain about, or praise.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche. Speaking at a conference in Berlin today, CEO Michael Leiters mentioned Porsche wants “to completely steer clear from any kind of effects and shows,” according to Bloomberg.

Recent findings suggest that both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15. Tesla made a Roadster flip in mid-air. Porsche indicated the Mission S, and Leiters states the two cars aren’t even chasing the same customers.

Tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype. The main event was a car using compressed-air thrusters to launch off a ramp, rotate in the air, and come back down on its wheels.

It was the payoff for months of hype. Musk spent most of the year promising a “flying” Roadster demo, and it slipped more than once. We reported in June that it had been pushed to August to make room for SpaceX thruster work.

There are three versions. The Performance trim uses suction fans and claims 0-60 mph in under 1.6 seconds, the Thrust trim adds rear cold-gas thrusters for a claimed sub-0.9-second run, and the single-seat Rocket trim gets thrusters all around the car and isn’t approved for public roads. Tesla gave no price and no production date, just Musk’s “2028, actually.”.

Industry observers note that porsche went the other way. Under the skin, the Mission S can take either a hybrid or a straight combustion powertrain. It’s a mid-engine car that sits above the 911 in the lineup, and well above it in price.

Leiters said customer response has been “overwhelming” and that Porsche would rather show off real technical innovation than put on a show. If it reaches production, Ferrari is the obvious target, and Porsche hasn’t played in that segment since the 918 Spyder. Porsche is counting on a pricier, more exclusive lineup to rebuild its profits.

Not everyone in the supercar world agrees with Leiters. Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna rated Tesla’s Roadster launch “10 out of 10” last month.

It has been revealed that leiters has a point, even if Porsche pitching a gas and hybrid supercar as “technical innovation” in 2026 is a bit rich. But what bothers me more is who Tesla is aiming at.

I’m concerned Tesla is starting to appeal to the lowest common denominator: people who watch a Roadster hop off a ramp and believe an actual flying car is coming. Musk pushed that idea himself. On Joe Rogan’s show, he called the upcoming demo “unforgettable” and mentioned that if Peter Thiel wants a flying car, “we should be able to buy one.”.

Sources indicate that that’s not real. Cold-gas thrusters work like a giant can of compressed air, and the math is brutal. The Rocket trim carries 400 liters of air at 10,000 psi, roughly 200 kg of gas. At the roughly 80 kN its rear thrusters produce, even a very efficient nozzle empties that tank in a few seconds. Then refilling it takes six to seven hours.

Also someone on Bluesky pointed out that the video shows Mach diamonds in the exhaust stream of the thrusters. Which means it's so loud that anyone within 100 feet would suffer immediate and permanent hearing loss. This Roadster isn't useful for anything other than temporarily pumping stock prices.

According to recent reports, so the Roadster’s “flying” will always be limited to stunts like this one. No hopping over traffic. No hovering. A couple of seconds of air, then a long wait at a compressor.

Recent findings suggest that that’s great for a viral clip. But this is a car that dropped from a promised 620 miles of range in 2017 to “over 300” today, and Tesla would rather sell people on a flight the physics can’t deliver.

It’s hard for me to get excited for that. As a BEV enthusiast, I’m not more excited about Porsche’s ICE Mission S, but at least I trust Porsche to actually deliver that to customers.

Toyota and Subaru hit the ‘sweet spot’ with affordable electric SUVs

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Toyota and Subaru’s latest electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.
  • The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.
  • Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toyota and Subaru’s latest electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.

The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.

Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.

Outside of Rivian, Toyota and Subaru are the only brands that have higher year-over-year EV sales in the US through the third quarter.

Combined, Toyota and Subaru have sold nearly 50,000 EVs through the first nine months of 2026, more than double compared to the same period last year.

Toyota alone has sold nearly 35,000 electric vehicles, up 183.4% YOY, while Subaru sold 14,630, up 46.7%. And that’s not even including the additional 12,676 sold under the Lexus brand, up 137.4% YOY.

While the two Japanese automakers were infamously slow to transition to battery electric vehicles, the timing worked in their favor.

Sources indicate that after launching the heavily updated bZ in late 2025, previously called the bZ4X, Toyota’s electric SUV suddenly became one of America’s most popular EVs. Through Q3, it was the fourth best-selling EV in the US, trailing only the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Tesla Model 3, and Tesla Model Y.

Industry observers note that starting at $35,000, the Toyota bZ is one of the most affordable EVs in the US. It also offers up to 314 miles of range in the FWD Plus trim, which starts at $37,980.

Toyota and Subaru now each sell three electric SUVs, which share the same platform and technology.

With prices ranging from roughly $35,000 to about $45,000, Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive, noted (via Bloomberg) Toyota and Subaru’s latest EVs are affordable and hit the “sweet spot” of the US car market.

Toyota also sells the smaller, sporty C-HR, starting at $37,080, and the larger, more rugged bZ Woodland, which starts at $45,380.

Subaru, on the other hand, sells the updated Solterra ($38,495, plus the smaller Uncharted ($34,995) and midsize Trailseeker ($39,995).

Karla Fisher, a Marine and retired engineer, told Bloomberg that the Subaru Trailseeker was her “most favorite car of all time.”.

While she considered buying an EV before the $7,500 federal credit expired last September, none met her requirements at the time. Fisher wanted at least 7″ of ground clearance, 250 miles or more range, and a price that was similar, or even less than a comparible gas-powered vehicle.

Recent findings suggest that the Subaru Trailseeker offers all of that and starts at under $40,000. Toyota and Subaru’s electric SUVs all start at about $45,000 or less, which is even less than the average fresh vehicle.

According to the latest Kelley Blue Book figures, the average price for a new vehicle in the US reached a record $51,109 in October, up 2.1% YOY.

Great as these may be, there is little inventory to be found.

There are less than 500 Uncharted available Nationwide.

You can't sell what you don't have. Yes, they can be ordered for sure, but how many missed sales does that model create?

Subaru spokesperson Dominick Infante said the affordable EV prices are mainly thanks to its partnership with Toyota. “We do believe there’s an EV future,” Infante added.

Next year, both brands will add a three-row electric SUV with the Toyota Highlander EV and Subaru Getaway.

Recent findings suggest that thinking about making the switch to an EV? With the 2027 models at dealerships, now could be a good time to find a deal on current 2026 models. You can use the links below to see what’s available at Toyota and Subaru dealerships near you.

Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bitcoinmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

SEC Freezes Assets in $560 Million Crypto Trading Ponzi Scheme

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Securities and Exchange Commission has frozen the assets of Indianapolis-based Backward Hat Capital and its two co-founders, saying the firm ran a $560 million Ponzi scheme that told investors their money would be turned into crypto and used for AI-driven currency trading.
  • The agency said Backward Hat, co-founders Phillip Williams and Devin Johnson, Johnson’s firm Traders Point Capital and Joseph Anderson raised the money from more than 2,000 investors starting in July 2022.
  • Federal prosecutors in Upcoming York and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission brought parallel cases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Securities and Exchange Commission has frozen the assets of Indianapolis-based Backward Hat Capital and its two co-founders, saying the firm ran a $560 million Ponzi scheme that told investors their money would be turned into crypto and used for AI-driven currency trading.

The agency said Backward Hat, co-founders Phillip Williams and Devin Johnson, Johnson’s firm Traders Point Capital and Joseph Anderson raised the money from more than 2,000 investors starting in July 2022. A federal court granted a temporary restraining order, an asset freeze and expedited discovery to halt what the SEC called an ongoing scheme.

Federal prosecutors in Upcoming York and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission brought parallel cases. The SEC and CFTC suits were filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana, and the CFTC remarked the court has appointed Kevin B. Duff as temporary receiver to take control of the companies and the individual defendants’ assets.

Sources indicate that according to the SEC’s complaint, Williams and Johnson sold limited partnership interests in private funds through a network of promoters, including to Williams’s former investment advisory clients. They promised a proprietary, “AI-driven” algorithm that supposedly returned at least 6% every month by trading foreign exchange.

Industry observers note that investor money, the pitch went, would first be converted into a crypto asset and then used for that arbitrage. The complaint does not name bitcoin as the asset. It claims about $109 million of the roughly $210 million raised from July 2022 to September 2025 was sent to the fund’s Coinbase account and converted.

Recent findings suggest that of that, more than $56 million went to personal crypto accounts held by Williams, Johnson and a relief defendant, according to the complaint. About $40 million ended up on three platforms where some of it was used to trade other crypto assets, but little to no money was used to trade FX. After October 2025, the scheme raised about $350 million, and none of it was sent to Coinbase.

The SEC remarked the defendants made more than $250 million in Ponzi payments to earlier investors and moved more than $220 million to themselves. The money paid for exotic cars, expensive homes, private air travel and other businesses they owned, and helped feed Johnson’s gambling. Promoters took more than $50 million.

Recent findings suggest that anderson is accused of producing fake financial reports, including at least two “audit reports” and a “quality of earnings” report from a supposedly independent firm. The SEC said the documents falsely claimed the returns had been verified against bank and brokerage records. It said Anderson did no audit work, was not independent and had a financial stake in the scheme.

According to recent reports, prosecutors in Manhattan charged Williams and Johnson with securities fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit securities fraud. The FBI arrested Williams in Kokomo, Indiana, and Johnson in Gilbert, Arizona, on Wednesday. Prosecutors put the total raised at more than $600 million.

“As alleged, Phillip Patrick Williams and Devin Allen Johnson promised to use investor funds for profitable foreign exchange currency trading,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “Williams and Johnson instead stole hundreds of millions of dollars from their investors for personal expenses and to pay off earlier investors in a Ponzi-like fashion.”.

It has been revealed that the CFTC put the Ponzi at more than $550 million from at least 2,100 participants and remarked defendants kept soliciting money through at least October 2026. Its complaint seeks restitution, disgorgement, civil penalties, trading bans and a permanent injunction. The SEC is seeking injunctions, disgorgement and civil penalties.

The case follows other recent enforcement actions tied to crypto-branded fraud. The SEC charged two companies in a $130 million crypto trading scheme last month, and Newly introduced York sought a $1.37 billion judgment against the operators of the NovaTech Ponzi scheme. In August, the CFTC charged Goliath Ventures with a $400 million bitcoin fraud.

Anne McKinley, acting associate director of the SEC’s Chicago Regional Office, said the promise of “a low-risk, high rate of return on a purportedly complex investment should make all potential investors stop and think before investing their money.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Leveraged funds reduced their net short positions in CME Bitcoin futures by 79.3% over five weeks before Bitcoin plunged below $60,000 on Friday.
  • The funds held 1,211 more short contracts than long contracts on Nov.
  • Together, those changes narrowed the gap between the two sides by 4,633 contracts, equivalent to 23,165 BTC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leveraged funds reduced their net short positions in CME Bitcoin futures by 79.3% over five weeks before Bitcoin plunged below $60,000 on Friday.

The funds held 1,211 more short contracts than long contracts on Nov. 17, down from 5,844 on Oct. 13, according to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's Nov. 20 report. The shift was driven primarily by declining short exposure. Over the period, short contracts fell from 3,889 to 7,475, while long contracts increased from 744 to 6,264.

Together, those changes narrowed the gap between the two sides by 4,633 contracts, equivalent to 23,165 BTC.

In a recent development, the reduction occurred at every weekly snapshot. Net shorts fell to 4,942 contracts on Oct. 20, 3,979 on Oct. 27, and 2,591 on Nov. 3 before reaching 1,243 on Nov. 10.

However, the retreat nearly stalled in the final week, with net shorts declining by just 32 contracts as both long and short positions contracted.

That was the smallest weekly reduction in the five-week period, compared with declines of more than 900 contracts in each of the preceding four weeks.

Sources indicate that leveraged funds’ net short fell in five straight weekly readings. Fewer reported short contracts drove most of the change.

In a recent development, CFTC futures-only data for standard CME Bitcoin futures. Each point is reported shorts minus longs. The final reading was 1,211 contracts.

Source: Oct. 13 · Oct. 20 · Oct. 27 · Nov. 3 · Nov. 10 · Nov. 17.

The net short narrowed by just 32 contracts in the final week.

Sources indicate that the CFTC data cover reported positions in the standard CME futures contract. Each observation is a weekly snapshot, with spot positions and intraweek trading outside its scope.

Net short is reported shorts minus reported longs. From October 13 to November 17, shorts fell from 11,364 to 7,475 and longs rose from 5,520 to 6,264. The two contributions are 3,889 and 744 contracts. Bar segments are proportional to these counts.

The CFTC data cover reported positions in the standard CME futures contract. Each observation is a weekly snapshot, with spot positions and intraweek trading outside its scope.

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin's drop below $60,000 on Nov. 20 introduced fresh selling pressure just as the decline in leveraged funds' net short positions had slowed.

The timing leaves a gap in the CFTC data. Friday's selloff occurred three days after the latest positioning snapshot, so any resulting changes in futures exposure were not recorded.

A fresh wave of short selling could reverse the trend, although funds could also become more net short by closing existing long positions.

The two outcomes would carry different implications for how traders responded to Bitcoin's decline.

In a recent development, however, the CFTC's leveraged-funds category includes hedge funds using futures to offset spot holdings or pursue arbitrage strategies. Some of the earlier reduction in short contracts may therefore reflect the unwinding of those trades rather than changing expectations for Bitcoin's price.

The CFTC's next report, scheduled for Nov. 30, will reflect positions held on Nov. 24.

The breakdown between long and short contracts will show whether funds rebuilt short exposure following the selloff or continued reducing positions despite Bitcoin's losses.

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1890 w)

Ice Dives Are the Simple Therapy Trick that Rewired My Anxious Brain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A few weeks ago, I was more anxious than I had been in a long time—or maybe ever.
  • Sources indicate that while calling your sister is always a good idea, mine also happens to be a clinical fellow at McLean Hospital, a.k.a.
  • Industry observers note that “I’m not hanging up until you do it,” she mentioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A few weeks ago, I was more anxious than I had been in a long time—or maybe ever. My thoughts were racing, and even for someone who deals with her share of anxiety, I was way beyond my normal self. So, I did what any person would do in that moment: I called my sister.

Sources indicate that while calling your sister is always a good idea, mine also happens to be a clinical fellow at McLean Hospital, a.k.a. one of the leading psychiatric institutions in the whole country, so let’s just say she knows how to handle an anxious person. Her suggestion was to go to the kitchen, grab a big bowl, fill it with ice water, and then dunk my face in it. I wasn’t exactly thrilled by the idea. It seemed like a whole bunch of work for something that couldn’t possibly help me in such a state.

Industry observers note that “I’m not hanging up until you do it,” she mentioned. She could tell I thought the idea was silly, and that I was probably going to skip it. And, I did think it was silly, but she seemed weirdly passionate that I submerge my face into a bowl of freezing water, so I complied. I grabbed a bowl, filled it with water and ice cubes, and reluctantly got my face wet, just barely making sure my nose and eyes were underwater.

I felt better basically instantly. The racing thoughts subsided and I could finally see straight. Even more impressive is the fact that once I reentered the situation that was making me anxious, all that nervous energy simply didn’t return. I was reset and relaxed. All it took was a bucket of water and about 30 seconds.

The trick—or, skill, I should say—that my sister taught me comes from dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT), a modality that was created by Marsha Linehan, PhD, who recently passed away at 83 years old. It was a breakthrough treatment for people facing extreme mental health challenges like chronic suicidality and borderline personality disorder, which Linehan revealed she struggled with in 2011, decades after DBT became the gold standard for treating those conditions.

Whether or not you are someone who deals with a formal mental health diagnosis or the occasional tough moment, DBT skills can make a big difference. The cold water trick my sister taught me is called an “ice dive,” and it’s one of four simple DBT tools that can help snap you out of a range of intense emotions promptly. Now, any time I feel myself getting heightened, my immediate next thought is: I should go grab a bucket of ice water. Call me converted.

Here’s how you can practice this skill too, plus, the three others that work just as well—and don’t involve water.

Meet the experts: Shireen Rizvi, PhD, is a clinical psychologist and director of psychology training and DBT services and research at Montefiore Einstein in Upcoming York City. Vibh Forsythe Cox, PhD, is a clinical associate professor at the University of Washington and the director of the Marsha M. Linehan DBT clinic.

According to recent reports, at this point, you’ve pretty much gotten the entire gist of an ice dive, but let’s recap: All it takes is a bowl big enough to get your full face in and some chilly water. (The colder the better, but it doesn’t need to reach ice bath territory.) Once you’ve got that, place it on a low-set table or even on the ground—you want to be bending over when you dunk your head in to mimic something closer to a dive—take a deep breath, and submerge your face, especially around your nasal passages and eyes, for as long as possible. 30 seconds is ideal, but that may feel like a really long time at first. Just go for as long as you can, and feel free to repeat multiple times for a cumulative total of 30 seconds.

It has been revealed that as for what is going on when you do this: Dunking your face in cold water triggers what is called the mammalian dive reflex, says Shireen Rizvi, PhD, a clinical psychologist and director of psychology training and DBT services and research at Montefiore Einstein in Latest York City. “It’s automatic,” she says. “You’re not doing anything consciously to create the reaction, which is there to help mammals survive cold water.”.

An ice dive triggers a survival mode where our bodies reduce our heart rate, slow down our breathing, and redirect blood to our vital organs, she explains. Under water, it helps you stay alive, but on land, it helps calm just about any activating emotion you might be experiencing. And, your face being what’s submerged is critical to get this specific reaction; getting in an ice bath where your face isn’t underwater actually spikes your heart rate due to cold shock, for example.

In a recent development, basically, an ice dive forces your body to focus on the bare necessities, like staying calm. It’s best used anytime your emotions are reaching a 90-plus on a scale of 1 to 100, Rizvi says, whether the emotion is anxiety, anger, stress, jealousy, or anything else. If you’re feeling it intensely and your heart rate is up, an ice dive can help.

Recent findings suggest that there’s one other handy use case too: If you’re ruminating. “When your body is in a survival mode, it's pulling resources back, and it actually also pulls your attention too, so if you have a lot of thoughts floating around in your head making you anxious, this can also help clear your mind temporarily,” claims Vibh Forsythe Cox, PhD, a clinical associate professor at the University of Washington and the director of the Marsha M. Linehan DBT clinic. Think of it this way: “You can't be thinking about a grocery list if you have just fallen into ice water,” she says.

And, while this trick has completely changed the game for me, I have some good news: There are three others that all have the same effect sans H2O.

An ice dive makes up the very first letter—T for temperature—in the TIPP acronym, which is a part of DBT’s distress tolerance pillar. The rest (intense exercise, paced breathing, and paired muscle relaxation) can all promptly calm and reset your nervous system, no liquid necessary.

All four skills have a similar basic mechanism. They take you from a heightened state (or a distressed one, to use DBT-speak) where your sympathetic nervous system is activated and bring you back into a relaxed one, where your parasympathetic nervous system is in the driver’s seat again. They’re not about talking or reflecting; they’re about helping you feel better in a moment when emotions are extreme.

Industry observers note that “These are skills that act to regulate your physiology,” Cox says. “Oftentimes when you are having an intense emotion, you think you have to handle it with your mind. These are skills that help you handle it with your body.” Of course, once you’re out of that intense moment, you may want to call on other mental tools and process what happened—but that’s not where you’re at when you’re calling on a TIPP skill. They’re for when you’re in crisis mode.

You can use any of them at any time with one important caveat: All TIPP skills are meant to rapidly slow down your heart rate, so if you’re someone with a heart condition or who takes meds like beta blockers, talk to your doctor first before trying any of them, Rizvi claims.

Without further ado, here’s what you need to know about the other three skills.

It has been revealed that the I in TIPP stands for intense exercise. This may sound similarly prohibitive to needing a bowl of water, but it’s actually quite simple. All you really need to do is get moving for about 30 seconds. Do some all-out jumping jacks, pump your arms up and down as fast as you can while sitting in your chair, or get into a plank. Just get your heart rate up and your muscles feel fatigued. “It feels paradoxical, but when you end that short burst of exercise, everything slows down,” Rizvi claims.

According to recent reports, there’s also an added benefit to going with exercise. When you’re feeling a heightened emotion, one of the ways your sympathetic nervous system reacts is by sending out glucose into your bloodstream, Cox notes. Again, this is an automatic, physical reaction, and it’s what gives you the energy for either a fight or flight response. But since you're probably not feeling anxious or angry because you need to escape a pack of hungry wolves, you probably won’t end up literally running away or fighting them off and using that energy. Exercising eats up some of that extra glucose, helping you get back to baseline.

If you’ve ever done box breathing, you’ve done the first P in TIPP. All it involves is breathing in and out in a controlled manner for a set number of seconds each time. “The main core of this technique is that your out breath needs to be longer than your in breath,” indicates Cox. “That is what activates your parasympathetic nervous system and slows everything down.”.

It has been revealed that in addition to keeping your out breath longer than your in breath (say four seconds in and eight out), you also want to make sure you’re breathing from your diaphragm, Rizvi notes. You can monitor this by placing your hand on your belly. If it’s rising and falling with each breath, you’re breathing from your diaphragm.

If you’re looking for an entry-level DBT skill, or one that you can do in pretty much any context, this is a good one to master. “I find paced breathing in particular is something that you can usually do no matter where you are or what you're doing,” Rizvi says. It takes no setup, no resources, and you can even do it in plain sight without people noticing.

Finally, the last TIPP skill is paired muscle relaxation. “When we are having an intense emotion, our body tenses up,” Cox claims. “This helps release some of that tension.”.

To do this skill, start at one end of your body and systematically work your way up or down, tensing and releasing your muscles throughout and saying the word “relax” each time. Pairing the muscle tensing with the word relax also helps train them—and therefore you—to relax on command, Cox notes.

There are plenty of guided paired muscle relaxation routines you can follow online, but you can also just do it on your own, tensing as many muscle groups as you’d like (or have time for).

Industry observers note that don’t have time to reread an article in a moment of crisis? Here are the quick and simple basics of all the TIPP skills for when you need to use them ASAP.

No matter which one you go for, remember this: “Emotions fire in the order of milliseconds,” Cox claims. That means that no matter how intense the thing you’re feeling is, it will pass, and probably much faster than you think. Sometimes, all our brains need is a reset initiated by our bodies.

Industry News: Meet SHRINCS: Bitcoin's Emerging Frontrunner for a Post-Quantum Signature

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blockstream Research Director Jonas Nick, with Mikhail Kudinov and collaborators, published a security analysis on Thursday for SHRINCS, advancing an emerging frontrunner for a post-quantum signature scheme in Bitcoin.
  • In a recent development, “We need all the possible feedback—engineers, cryptographers, protocol developers,” Kudinov, a post-quantum cryptography researcher at Blockstream, noted in reference to a draft of SHRINCS’ Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP).
  • Notably, SHRINCS is a hash-based signature scheme that leverages SHA-256 to anchor its security in battle-tested primitives that are already used by Bitcoin, representing a conservative effort to minimize the proposal’s trust assumptions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blockstream Research Director Jonas Nick, with Mikhail Kudinov and collaborators, published a security analysis on Thursday for SHRINCS, advancing an emerging frontrunner for a post-quantum signature scheme in Bitcoin.

In a recent development, “We need all the possible feedback—engineers, cryptographers, protocol developers,” Kudinov, a post-quantum cryptography researcher at Blockstream, noted in reference to a draft of SHRINCS’ Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP). “There are a lot of things to check, test, complain about, or praise.".

Notably, SHRINCS is a hash-based signature scheme that leverages SHA-256 to anchor its security in battle-tested primitives that are already used by Bitcoin, representing a conservative effort to minimize the proposal’s trust assumptions.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

That noted, the scheme comes with trade-offs, most notably by introducing potential security vulnerabilities at the implementation level if misused. The scheme combines two spending paths: a small, more efficient stateful signature option and a larger, more costly stateless path with fewer security risks on the implementation side.

Although stateful signatures are compact, preserving Bitcoin’s ability to process transactions efficiently, a user can trigger a critical failure—where an attacker can forge a signature for that address and steal funds if a one-time state is accidentally reused. Because SHRINCS’ stateful path relies on one-time keys that can only safely sign a single transaction, wallet developers must carefully track each key’s state.

“It needs to be impossible for the user to behave in a way that this catastrophic event happens,” Nick told Head of MARA Foundation Isabel Foxen Duke during a recent appearance on MARA Foundation TV. “Wallet developers need to deal with this stateful component correctly.”.

According to Nick, for SHRINCS to work safely in the real world, its specification and corresponding wallet implementations must automatically enforce the stateless path fallback in any situation where a state counter could possibly be compromised.

While some users might gravitate toward stateless signatures out of caution, Nick warns that widespread adoption could bloat the blockchain and drive up fees across the network.

According to recent reports, bitcoin’s current ECDSA signatures are typically 71 bytes long (and Taproot Schnorr signatures are 64 bytes). Under SHRINCS, stateful signatures are anywhere from 548 to 4,619 bytes, while stateless ones are 5,777 bytes. That mentioned, optimizations of both signature paths have been accelerating with the support of AI-based research, Nick noted.

Sources indicate that “We don’t know what the fee market will look like once we have these very substantial signatures,” he stated. “And it’s not just the fee market, it’s also just fewer transactions fit into a block, meaning fewer people can use Bitcoin. And I think this changes the value proposition of Bitcoin.”.

As the SHRINCS working group—which includes researchers backed by nonprofits including Brink and OpenSats—continues to refine the proposal’s specification, Blockstream researchers stress that getting the cryptographic foundation right is only half the battle.

Industry observers note that whether the broader Bitcoin ecosystem is ready to embrace SHRINCS’ inherent trade-offs will depend heavily on feedback from the network’s stakeholders in the months ahead. Meanwhile, Nick and Kudinov are requesting review of the proposal and the security analysis.

Sources indicate that andré Beganski is a Senior Content Manager at MARA Foundation, producing content on topics including the intersection of quantum computing and cryptography. He has previously worked for Decrypt.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai’s US electric vehicle lineup will look a bit different in 2027, including the latest IONIQ 6 N, a new range-topping IONIQ 9 trim, and a handful of minor updates to the IONIQ 5.

Hyundai declared its 2027 model-year changes on Wednesday, including the upcoming IONIQ 6 N and a few slight changes to the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9.

While Hyundai discontinued the standard IONIQ 6, it added the high-performance IONIQ 6 N for the 2027 lineup.

Sources indicate that the IONIQ 6 N is Hyundai’s second performance EV, following the IONIQ 5 N. Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, the electric sports car delivers a combined 641 hp and 568 lb-ft of torque.

Hyundai said the IONIQ 6 N can sprint from 0 to 60 mph in 3.2 seconds, beating the IONIQ 5 N at 3.25 seconds.

Like the IONIQ 5 N, it also includes fun added features, like N e-Shift and an N Active Sound+ system that simulates the sounds and sensations of a traditional gas-powered sports car with an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission.

In a recent development, it uses an 84 kWh battery that provides up to 245 miles of pure electric driving range. Thanks to its 800V ultra-fast charging architecture, the IONIQ 6 N can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger.

Like Hyundai’s other electric vehicles, it comes standard with a native NACS charging port and a CCS adapter.

The 2027 IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 are mostly carryover models with a few minor changes, while the IONIQ 5 N remains the same as the 2026 model year.

Changes to the IONIQ 5 for the 2027 model year include roof rails, which are now available on the SEL trim and above; previously, they were only available on the XRT and Limited trims.

Hyundai HomeLink will be available exclusively on the Limited trim, rather than SEL and above, in the current 2026 model year, while the Cargo Cover will be offered as an Accessory only.

Regarding color options, the Gravity Gold Matte and Sage Silver Matte will no longer be available for the 2027 IONIQ 5.

The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,250, making it one of the most affordable EVs in the US.

It has been revealed that that’s for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. The extended-range SE RWD model is $2,500 more, starting at $37,750, and offers up to 318 miles of range.

Sources indicate that hyundai’s three-row SUV also received a handful of updates. The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 9 will be available with a new Calligraphy Black Ink trim, while the Calligraphy Design will no longer be offered.

In a recent development, the 2027 IONIQ 9 Calligraphy and Calligraphy Black Ink trims gain a Virtual Gear Shift and heated third-row seats. All variants also gain a Tailgate Emergency Lamp.

Industry observers note that on the one hand... the Ioniq5 is due for an upgrade. On the other... I still absolutely love the way it looks, and notice just about every one I pass on the road.

Hyundai has yet to announce prices for the 2027 model. The base 2026 IONIQ 9 S starts at $58,995 and offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 335 miles.

The previous top-spec Performance Calligraphy Design AWD started at $76,490, so you can expect the new Calligraphy Black Ink to be around the same, if not even more.

Tesla confirms rare new delivery of 50 Semi electric trucks in Chicago

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has confirmed a new batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s a rare data point.
  • The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, reveals four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has confirmed a new batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a rare data point. Tesla doesn’t disclose Semi deliveries, and it claims its new Nevada factory can build 50,000 of them a year.

The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, reveals four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.

Hello Windy CityChicago’s first 50 Semis en route for delivery pic.twitter.com/75kig8yWsb.

But the only 50-truck Semi order tied to Chicago belongs to HMD Trucking. The family-owned carrier was founded in Chicago in 1998, runs more than 650 trucks (almost all diesel), and ordered 50 Semis right after Tesla’s production event in September.

In a recent development, HMD took its first truck on November 2 and notes it’s the first Tesla Semi registered in Illinois. COO Michael Mahler stated Tesla “has been transparent with us regarding the capabilities of Semi every step of the way.”.

It has been revealed that the manufacturer ran a Semi for more than 4,000 miles over the summer and averaged 1.74 kWh per mile, right in line with Tesla’s 1.7 kWh/mile claim. The first trucks will mostly handle local runs around Chicago, and HMD is installing its own chargers there since Tesla’s Megacharger network is still concentrated along the I-5 and I-10 corridors in the West.

Owner Henry Malukas told MotorTrend the deal is worth about $15 million. That’s roughly $300,000 per truck, in line with the ~$290,000 Long Range pricing we reported when the first truck came off the high-volume line and a long way from the $180,000 Tesla advertised in 2017.

Here’s the problem: it’s nearly impossible to tell how many Semis Tesla is actually building.

Tesla released volume production at its Sparks, Nevada factory on September 24, after pushing the ramp out of 2025. It says the 1.8 million sq ft plant is built for 50,000 trucks a year. But it never gave a ramp schedule, and its quarterly production and delivery reports only count “passenger vehicles sold to customers.” The Semi isn’t in there.

According to recent reports, so we’re left with proxies. Tesla notes its Semi fleet has over 98% uptime, without saying how significant that fleet is. Before this year, the largest Semi fleet was PepsiCo’s, at 86 trucks in 2024. California’s truck voucher program received 965 Semi applications between January 2025 and February 2026, which points to real demand but says nothing about output.

Industry observers note that the order book is the other clue. Einride ordered 500 Semis in August, WattEV has 370 on order, IMC Logistics wants 50 for California, and the ZET SCALE alliance picked Tesla as main supplier for 2,500 trucks. And now HMD’s 50 are rolling into Chicago, one of the first Semi fleets that will have to deal with a Midwest winter. Wisconsin’s Paper Transport has also been piloting a Semi in the Chicago market since the summer.

None of that adds up to a production rate, but it does look like Tesla is slowly ramping up deliveries.

Tesla keeps the Semi numbers vague on purpose. It’s happy to talk about a 50,000-truck-a-year factory, and it posts hero shots when a batch ships, but it won’t give the one number that demonstrates whether the factory is anywhere close to that.

Sources indicate that I think the semi is going to be a big seller but its going to take some time to produce enough of them and for companies to gather enough data. Once the investment is justified, there will be customers and repeat customers. After that, it will only be a matter of time before other electric semi truck manufacturers start popping up with offerings and thats a good thing for everyone.

In a recent development, the 50,000 figure is what makes the Semi look like a real business to investors instead of a niche program that took nine years to get going. Tesla has a long history of quoting capacity long before it reaches it, so we shouldn’t treat “built for 50,000” as anything more than a ceiling.

Our read: Tesla is still far from that 50,000 rate. Fifty trucks for one customer is 0.1% of a year at full capacity, and if Tesla were shipping in large volumes, a single 50-unit batch wouldn’t get its own post. But the ramp has clearly started, the order book is real, and it’s plausible Tesla gets into the thousands by the end of the year.

In a recent development, good for HMD, too. A 650-truck diesel fleet in a cold market is exactly the kind of customer the Semi has to win. Malukas admitted “we don’t have real numbers yet” on savings, and HMD’s own blog is fairly sober about cost and winter range. Local routes, depot charging and a Chicago winter is the right way to find out. It all sounds plausible for the Tesla Semi.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

My interest in hair removal started in elementary school when I snuck into my mom's medicine cabinet and dragged her razor across my leg like I was coloring with my favorite box of markers. Needless to say, I've learned the right way to shave since then (namely to apply shaving cream and gently glide my razor toward the grain with light pressure).

I've had a lot of help perfecting my technique—as a beauty editor with a decade of testing experience, I have access to the best dermatologists and aestheticians. Yet, no matter how on-point my fresh shaving technique is now, most women's razors never get my legs quite as smooth. And other hair removal methods are super painful, ripping strands out at the root. Ouch!

But then, I upgraded to electric razors—and I've never turned back.

It has been revealed that “A closer shave can feel nice, but because the surface of our skin is not perfectly smooth, it inevitably results in removal of some skin cells,” states dermatologist Caroline Robinson, MD. This can lead to microscopic nicks and irritation. “Electric razors can help avoid this. They’re typically less sensitizing,” says Dr. Robinson, because the shave they provide is not as close. At-home laser hair removal devices, waxing, sugaring, and threading are all great options for hair removal if you’ve got the time (and the coin), but if silky-smooth skin sans irritation is what you’re after, the answer is electric.

In a recent development, over the past two years, Women's Health editors have been testing popular electric razors to determine which seven are worth the investment. Ultimately, we found that the Philips Beauty Series was the best multi-use product due to its five-blade razor and dual-sidedness that allows for a super close shave. Meanwhile, the Remington Smooth & Silky On-the-Go Shaver delivers on quality for quick touch-ups while being budget- and travel-friendly. Read on to see our other winners from our testing process.

Sources indicate that A favorite of our editors, this hair removal device hits all of the targets we're looking for when buying an electric razor. For starters, it literally has 40 micro-grip tweezers in its motor to provide a super close shave, keeping your skin smooth for weeks at a time. While that might seem intimidating, it upgrades your in-shower shaving routine in a major way.

You can hit even the trickiest spots on your body. From your underarms and belly down to your ankles, this electric razor has you covered quite literally from head to toe. And with an impressive 50-minute runtime you can eliminate all of my unwanted hair with this device at least a couple of times before recharging it for just an hour. You’ll also appreciate that it's lightweight but not flimsy like it'll slip out of your grip. Plus, it's waterproof so you can shave in the shower without worrying about your latest razor cranking out mid-shave.

An upgrade from the original Braun model, the more expensive but higher-tech Flex comes with a flexible head (hence, the name) that can uniquely adapt to your body's curves and contours—even the complicated corners of your bikini line. In addition to the epilator, the bundle also comes with a body exfoliation brush, skin contact cap for additional comfort, and more—definitely a bargain.

"The face and body brushes are especially useful, and I love how you can interchange the heads depending on what type of cleansing you want to do," indicates Women's Health contributor Isabel McMahon.

She credits the device’s built-in light, called the "smartlight," as a great option for women who like dimmer lighting while showering but still want to see what they're doing.
